comment_text.value:
Co-author here - first paper from my postdoc accepted to NeurIPS main conference.

We built a way to sample diverse ideas in machine learning - ideas that make scientific sense, but that no existing research community is positioned to propose.

In short, the way it works is like this:

1. Take 16,068 LLM papers (NeurIPS, ICLR, ICML, ACL, EMNLP, 2017 to 2025) are broken into 273 "idea atoms". Every paper, and every candidate idea, becomes a set of atoms.

2. Train a Coherence Model: a 42.8M-parameter transformer trained on papers as sequences of atoms. Basically a language model whose tokens are ideas.

3. Train a Cognitive-Availability Model: a dual encoder trained on the publication histories of 39,791 researchers, which predicts where each person could plausibly go next.

4. Use those models to score sampled tuples using reciprocal rank fusion (you want ideas that go together well, but that are not cognitively available to anyone).

We tested it in a bunch of ways. One interesting one was that we took all the papers at the end of 2024, then checked which high-scoring tuples showed up in 2025 papers. It worked well - one examples is an ICLR 2025 oral, goes from rank 1,489 with coherence alone to the top 25 of 1.14M samples.

A funny one: if you ask Claude to come up with an ML research idea, it is often about interpretability. If you then run an autoresearch pipeline with some A100s on the idea, the result tends to be interpretability 8/10 times. Our Alien Sampling method stayed at 0 interpretability ideas even after letting claude cook on them.

We also paid 50 people with graduate degrees in CS/AI to judge the research reports and found that Alien’s reports had the best average quality rank and produced 3 of the top 5 reports.

Oh and then we scaled it way the hell up to a couple million papers and 10,000,000's of concept elements and generated 25,000 new research proposals that you can search over here: https://lacuna.tiptreesystems.com/explore?view=hypotheses

Code (MIT): https://github.com/alejandrohdez00/alien-space-of-science

story_title.value: The alien space of science: Coherent but cognitively unavailable directions

comment_text.value:
I feel for everyone in this situation. I don't think anyone is wrong to mourn the undeniably massive shift happening to something that has been such a big part of our lives, and I don't think anyone is wrong to be excited. I say this as someone who has worked in ML for coming up on 10 years now and is more towards the latter camp, where I love working with agents, and still spend plenty of time writing code by hand and studying. I don't think it's fair to pretend people are being unreasonable or are just "missing the big picture" for being unhappy.

But I also have found that where you work and what AI usage is like in your company is a pretty big deciding factor. Your comment, which I agree with, made me think about this. I consult a decent amount, and I've worked with companies where the engineering culture has adopted AI in a way I describe as "ugly." I should find a better word. But what I mean is that it's sort of like the attitude is "okay, now we can ship more tickets, so everyone take on 8x the workload". And they do a lot of "best practice" kind of stuff around using coding agents--every new anthropic article gets posted to slack, and there's always a new CI process for using agents--but they're fundamentally just trying to do the same work as before but kinda sorta faster. It's a weirdly miserable experience.

On the other hand, I've worked with companies where the engineering culture almost feels exuberant. I think a consistent difference is that in these companies, it feels like the engineers now have permission to try wildly ambitious things. It's not always optimally productive in the sense that more things get thrown away or end up just not really working out, but overall they move significantly faster and do more interesting work. Commonly, it's things they wanted to do before, but simply weren't realistic with their constraints around capacity. Or it's an idea like "this part of the codebase has always been a performance nightmare, but it's also a beast to untangle. I wonder if I could setup an autoresearch loop and let it run all day, even just to harvest some ideas?"

But yeah, when everyone sort of gives up and/or are forced to move an ungodly number of smaller tickets, it is a miserable time.

story_title.value: It's still ok to enjoy programming

And setting up an autoresearch system and running it overnight will get you expert level optimizations if you set the metric up right.

These things excel at performance optimizations.

They just merged my PR for the current tightest bound on the integer multiplication problem:

https://github.com/CrocSwap/integer-mult-bounds/pull/37#even...

Something interesting happened last night: Researchers started proposing tighter conditional bounds for integer multiplication, submitted by OpenAI yesterday, then a swarm of collaborators online pushed it even further. Its so interesting that human researchers provided the insights to push to the out-of distribution solutions that no one model reached alone.

I just submitted the current new best conditional bound, conditional κ = 4.123863984e-5, and I have a very useful system setup for auto-research that requires human intuition to reach out-of-distribution solutions.

I have a list of ideas to test so we may not be done yet :) Original paper from OpenAI: https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/Integer-m...

comment_text.value:
I actually disagree that software is a static program. If a program always have the same behaviour, it's a pretty bad program. You need inputs and, as demonstrated by the recent LLM inputs, parameters you can tune to correctly address a specific context.

I would also contest the point about science being social. To me, science is the interplay between social constructions and physical reality. Which is why tests and experiments are so fundamental. Your point about software development as kind of like science is spot on: why not be exploratory/empirical in software development? Couldn't we imagine an LLM, say, that would go out and try to solve a question we frame? This seems strikingly close to autoresearch [1]

[1]: https://github.com/karpathy/autoresearch

story_title.value: Science Is Open Software

What I feel a bit annoyed by, and what I feel obviously LLM-run ablations like this fail to capture, is any kind of reflection around previous research or any kind of proof that this is the best you can do. You don't know, you pulled the lever and you got something, is the best? Can you do better? What is the constraint?

As an individual researcher, you do not have 22M$ to run a massive brute-force search for your problem. You are constrained to your little subscription and you will barely dip your toe in the sea of possible solutions to a problem. So letting Claude run an autoresearch loop on your problem and then having it summarize it for you brings 0 value because you dont know what the downsides and trade-offs of LRU caches were, and how you would possible solve it.

story_title.value: LRU is harder to beat than the KV-cache papers suggest

comment_text.value:
RSI is a fetishistic term among the singularity crowd, who imagine AI "recursively" improving itself in some exponential fashion until there is a bright flash of white light and it reveals itself in the form of god. Or something like that.

I don't know why whoever coined the term chose "recursive" rather than "iterative" - just sounds more likely to lead to infinite regress I suppose.

This notion of recursive/iterative self-improvement, whereby generation #1 AI improves itself to create generation #2, then generation #2 further improves itself to create generation #3, etc, seems to conflict with the reality that what we have with LLMs is models whose performance/capability is defined by data, not code, so the most you can do is have your LLM design synthetic data, or just do Karpathy-style "auto research" where all you are doing is using the LLM to automate your experiments.

At the end of the day, each experiment, designed by a person and/or LLM, then needs to compete with all your other ideas for compute to be tested at scale, and no amount of recursion or self-improvement will materialize an infinite amount of compute out of thin air, so your recursively synthetic-data gobbling LLM will continue to improve at the same pace it ever did.

story_title.value: Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI

comment_text.value: My experiment is examining the autonomy of Fable specifically in an auto research context. I don't believe I said in my message that no other model would have been able to complete my highly autonomous work. So it feels like my view has been misrepresented or misunderstood. This message makes it harder for me to share the things that excite me online and makes it more daunting to share my findings when this project completes, especially any comparative work. For an analogy, I feel like I said that I like Southern Butter Pecan Ice Cream and am being met with a response of the form "Sounds a bit sad that you have to wait for a weekly restock to enjoy any ice cream." I made a goal for myself to be more open with my feelings in life and share more of what I'm working on and not be so rejection-sensitive. I understand that even if I'm just sharing the positivity I feel, it can come across differently. I guess this is just the cost of communication in a lossy language.

comment_text.value:
It still feels pretty slow, and I see some low-hanging fruit:

- in safari, every image is loaded twice, .heic and .webp

- default.png is re-downloaded 31 times, uncached

- images below the fold are request immediately, lazy loading would avoid that [1]

But most important, you have 229 requests for tiny files being served over HTTP 1.1. Without GZIP. From a pretty slow server - 700ms+ to download the main json data. Bundling your JS, or enabling HTTP2 or QUIC/HTTP3 alone would massively improve performance.

If this is the result of days of autoresearch, it's not really anything to celebrate.

[1] https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/...

story_title.value: There's no reason for software to be slow anymore

This speaks to me. I've been running an autoresearch loop the past couple of days to improve the load time of my various projects' frontends.
